chunks.text: 2 Methodology As illustrated in Fig. 3 , DeBoneDiT is a two-stage framework for high-resolution bone suppression. In the first stage, we introduce Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE) to compress high-dimensional images into latent representations, incorporating a multi-level depth feature loss to preserve structural consistency. In the second stage, we formulate the bone suppression task as a Brownian bridge diffusion process by establishing a direct bridge between the source CXR distribution and the target soft tissue distribution, effectively narrowing the inter-domain gap. This process is further enhanced by Source Condition Injection (SCI), which leverages the source CXR as explicit structural guidance to mitigate anatomical drift and error accumulation. 2.1 Depth Auto-Encoder To explicitly preserve structural information during latent compression, we propose Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE) as a structure-aware vision tokenizer. Unlike conventional tokenizers that focus solely on surface-level reconstruction fidelity, DAE incorporates a multi-level depth feature loss derived from the pretrained Depth Anything V2 encoder, enabling it to preserve both visual fidelity and structural consistency. Specifically, the DAE comprises an encoder E E , a decoder D D , a codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} , a discriminator 𝒟 adv \mathcal{D}_{\text{adv}} , and a pretrained depth feature extractor ϕ \phi . Given an input CXR or soft tissue image x ∈ ℝ 1 × H × W x\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times H\times W} , the encoder maps it into a continuous latent representation z e = E ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ C × H r × W r z_{e}=E(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times\frac{H}{r}\times\frac{W}{r}} , where r r denotes the downsampling factor. Subsequently, z e z_{e} is quantized against the codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} to obtain the discrete latent representation z = 𝒬 ⁡ ( z e ) ∈ ℝ C × H r × W r z=\mathcal{Q}(z_{e})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times\frac{H}{r}\times\frac{W}{r}} , where 𝒬 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{Q}(\cdot) denotes the vector quantization operator.

The decoder then reconstructs the image x ^ = D ⁡ ( z ) \hat{x}=D(z) . Furthermore, the discriminator 𝒟 adv \mathcal{D}_{\text{adv}} distinguishes real from reconstructed images to drive the recovery of sharp, high-fidelity details. Following the established latent space construction [ 30 , 31 ] , the objective function of DAE combines a composite reconstruction loss ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} and supplementary constraints: ℒ DAE = ℒ rec + ℒ qua + λ adv ​ ℒ adv , \mathcal{L}_{\text{DAE}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{qua}}+\lambda_{\text{adv}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}, (1) where ℒ qua \mathcal{L}_{\text{qua}} and ℒ adv \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}} represent the standard vector quantization loss [ 7 ] and multi-scale adversarial loss [ 35 ] , respectively. Specifically, we define the reconstruction loss by integrating the depth feature loss with traditional pixel-wise and perceptual constraints: ℒ rec = ℒ MSE + λ per ​ ℒ per + λ dep ​ ℒ dep , \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\lambda_{\text{per}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{per}}+\lambda_{\text{dep}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{dep}}, (2) where ℒ MSE \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} and ℒ per \mathcal{L}_{\text{per}} denote the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss and VGG-16-based perceptual loss [ 15 ] , respectively. In this work, we utilize the pretrained Depth Anything V2 [ 36 ] encoder as the depth feature extractor ϕ \phi . All the images were resized to 1024 × \times 1024 pixels for experimental consistency. SZCH-X-Rays comprises 741 pairs of posterior-anterior CXR and DES soft tissue images, acquired using a GE Discovery XR656 system in collaboration with our partner hospital. Initially stored in 14-bit DICOM format, the images were converted to PNG format to streamline the processing workflow, which feature an original resolution of 2021 × 2021 2021\times 2021 with a pixel size of 0.194 mm. Consistent with prior studies [ 2 , 38 ] , examinations affected by operational errors, pronounced motion artifacts, severe pleural effusion, or pneumothorax were excluded because these conditions may substantially degrade the quality of DES soft tissue references. Finally, the dataset was partitioned into 592 training, 74 validation and 75 test pairs. The dataset is publicly available under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license. JSRT contains 241 pairs of CXR and synthetic soft tissue images, split into 192 training, 24 validation and 25 test pairs. The CXR images were sourced from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology while the corresponding soft tissue images were algorithmically synthesized by researchers at the Budapest University of Technology and Economics. The original images feature a resolution of 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 pixels.

Asraf encompasses 6939 posterior-anterior CXR images sourced from publicly available resources, evenly distributed across three diagnostic classes with 2313 images each: pneumonia, COVID-19, and normal. Original resolutions vary from 205 × 138 205\times 138 to 5623 × 4757 5623\times 4757 pixels, with 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 being the most prevalent size at 45.2%. To prevent distortion in the non-square images, we cropped each to its maximum square. To evaluate clinical applicability, we performed downstream classification on this dataset using a 5-fold cross-validation strategy to ensure robustness. 3.1.2 Evaluation Metrics We employ five main quantitative metrics to evaluate the bone suppression performance, including Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [ 40 ] ( ↓ \downarrow ), Mean Squared Error (MSE) ( ↓ \downarrow ), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) ( ↑ \uparrow ), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) ( ↑ \uparrow ), and Bone Suppression Ratio (BSR) [ 13 ] ( ↑ \uparrow ), a metric that specifically measures the proportion of bone signal effectively suppressed relative to the original bone energy. For downstream task evaluation, we report four classification metrics, namely accuracy ( ↑ \uparrow ), precision ( ↑ \uparrow ), recall ( ↑ \uparrow ), and F1-score ( ↑ \uparrow ). Additionally, we utilize the Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator (BRISQUE) [ 19 ] ( ↓ \downarrow ) to evaluate the quality of both generated images and ground truth. 3.2 Implementation Details All experiments were performed using PyTorch 2.5.1 on an NVIDIA A800 GPU within Ubuntu 22.04. The DAE was trained from scratch for 200 epochs with a batch size of 4 using the Adam optimizer. Specifically, the learning rate was set to 10 − 4 10^{-4} for both the encoder E E and decoder D D , and 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for the discriminator 𝒟 adv \mathcal{D}_{\text{adv}} .

Regarding the latent space, the downsampling factor r r and the channel dimension C C were set to 4, resulting in a latent representation of z ∈ ℝ 4 × 256 × 256 z\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 256\times 256} for input x ∈ ℝ 1 × 1024 × 1024 x\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 1024\times 1024} . The codebook 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} was configured with a size of K = 1024 K=1024 . For the depth feature extractor ϕ \phi , we adopted the ViT-B/14 configuration, with input data resized to 518 × 518 518\times 518 pixels prior to depth feature extraction. Consequently, the sequence length of spatial patch tokens was N p = 1369 N_{\text{p}}=1369 , and the feature dimensions D l D_{l} for the L = 4 L=4 selected intermediate layers were 96, 192, 384, and 768, respectively. To balance different training objectives, the trade-off weights for DAE training were set to λ adv = 10 − 2 \lambda_{\text{adv}}=10^{-2} , λ per = 10 − 3 \lambda_{\text{per}}=10^{-3} , and λ dep = 1 \lambda_{\text{dep}}=1 . In addition, the DiT-based denoising network ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} with N = 12 N=12 DiT blocks was trained from scratch for 2000 epochs with a batch size of 8 using the AdamW optimizer. Specifically, a multi-step learning rate decay strategy was employed, initialized at 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Following established practices [ 30 ] , Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [ 11 ] were adopted to ensure model robustness during training and inference, respectively. Furthermore, the number of diffusion timesteps T T was set to 1000 for training, whereas only 50 sampling steps were utilized for inference to facilitate rapid generation. For the downstream evaluation, all five classification models were fine-tuned from ImageNet-1K [ 25 ] pretrained weights using the Adam optimizer with a weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . The initial learning rate was set to 10 − 3 10^{-3} with a plateau-based learning rate scheduler.

All these models were trained for 20 epochs with a batch size of 16 using the standard cross-entropy loss with a label smoothing coefficient of 0.15. 3.3 Main Results We conduct a rigorous quantitative evaluation against seven state-of-the-art methods, encompassing conventional GAN-based Yang et al. First, owing to the inherent physical constraints of 2D projections, when pathological features are completely occluded by hyperdense bony structures, the model’s reconstruction relies on learned generative priors, which may introduce hallucinations or omit extremely subtle lesions. Second, while the Depth Anything V2 encoder provides effective structural regularization, it was trained on natural images. Future work could explore CT-derived supervision to learn anatomy-aware, projection-consistent structural representations. Third, although the SZCH-X-Rays dataset establishes a high-quality benchmark, our evaluation is currently retrospective and limited to single-center data. Multi-site external validation and prospective clinical studies would further strengthen the assessment of the model’s generalizability and clinical utility. 3.1 Datasets and Evaluation metrics 3.1.1 Data Preparation We conducted comprehensive experiments across three distinct datasets, with each dataset assigned a specific role in evaluation: our self-constructed SZCH-X-Rays dataset and the publicly available JSRT dataset [ 27 ] were utilized for performance evaluation, while the Asraf dataset [ 1 ] was employed for downstream evaluation to benchmark clinical applicability. All the images were resized to 1024 × \times 1024 pixels for experimental consistency. SZCH-X-Rays comprises 741 pairs of posterior-anterior CXR and DES soft tissue images, acquired using a GE Discovery XR656 system in collaboration with our partner hospital.

Initially stored in 14-bit DICOM format, the images were converted to PNG format to streamline the processing workflow, which feature an original resolution of 2021 × 2021 2021\times 2021 with a pixel size of 0.194 mm. Consistent with prior studies [ 2 , 38 ] , examinations affected by operational errors, pronounced motion artifacts, severe pleural effusion, or pneumothorax were excluded because these conditions may substantially degrade the quality of DES soft tissue references. Finally, the dataset was partitioned into 592 training, 74 validation and 75 test pairs. The dataset is publicly available under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license. JSRT contains 241 pairs of CXR and synthetic soft tissue images, split into 192 training, 24 validation and 25 test pairs. The CXR images were sourced from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology while the corresponding soft tissue images were algorithmically synthesized by researchers at the Budapest University of Technology and Economics. The original images feature a resolution of 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 pixels. Asraf encompasses 6939 posterior-anterior CXR images sourced from publicly available resources, evenly distributed across three diagnostic classes with 2313 images each: pneumonia, COVID-19, and normal. Original resolutions vary from 205 × 138 205\times 138 to 5623 × 4757 5623\times 4757 pixels, with 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 being the most prevalent size at 45.2%. To prevent distortion in the non-square images, we cropped each to its maximum square. To evaluate clinical applicability, we performed downstream classification on this dataset using a 5-fold cross-validation strategy to ensure robustness.

First, owing to the inherent physical constraints of 2D projections, when pathological features are completely occluded by hyperdense bony structures, the model’s reconstruction relies on learned generative priors, which may introduce hallucinations or omit extremely subtle lesions. Second, while the Depth Anything V2 encoder provides effective structural regularization, it was trained on natural images. Future work could explore CT-derived supervision to learn anatomy-aware, projection-consistent structural representations. Third, although the SZCH-X-Rays dataset establishes a high-quality benchmark, our evaluation is currently retrospective and limited to single-center data. Multi-site external validation and prospective clinical studies would further strengthen the assessment of the model’s generalizability and clinical utility. 4 Conclusion In this paper, we present DeBoneDiT, a depth-driven bridge diffusion Transformer achieving high-fidelity bone suppression with remarkable computational efficiency on standard CXR images. To mitigate data scarcity, we introduce SZCH-X-Rays, the largest high-quality paired dataset for bone suppression to date. By integrating structure-aware latent compression, a source-conditioned Brownian bridge diffusion process, and a DiT-based denoising network, our framework effectively preserves critical pulmonary textures while maintaining rapid inference. Extensive experiments and downstream evaluation demonstrate that DeBoneDiT achieves superior performance with reduced computational overhead, underscoring its potential as a practical tool for clinical CXR bone suppression.
